title: SQL Injection Attack Lab - System Security TP
description: Practical work (TP) based on the SEED Labs "SQL Injection Attack Lab". Students exploit SQL injection vulnerabilities in a vulnerable employee-management web application (SELECT and UPDATE statements), then fix the vulnerability with a prepared statement.
prerequisites: Basic Linux command line and SSH
outcomes: Understand how SQL injection vulnerabilities arise from unsanitized input.
Exploit SQL injection in a SELECT statement to bypass authentication.
Exploit SQL injection in an UPDATE statement to modify unauthorized data.
Explain why stacked queries are blocked in this setup.
Fix a SQL injection vulnerability using prepared statements.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# SQL Injection Attack Lab

This training is based on the **SEED Labs "SQL Injection Attack Lab"** (copyright (c) 2006-2020 Wenliang Du, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), used here as the practical work (TP) of the System Security course.

You will attack a vulnerable Employee Management web application (`www.seed-server.com`) running in Docker containers on your sandbox, then fix the vulnerability using prepared statements.

**Rules**
- Every level has its own flag. Flags are unique to your sandbox and case-sensitive: do not share them, and do not accept flags from another student.
- Using a hint costs points (shown on each level). Viewing the solution also costs points on all training levels.
- The scenario is scored out of **200 points** (your grade out of 20 is `score / 10`).
- This is an educational exercise. Do not use these techniques outside of this sandbox.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Connect to your sandbox, then submit **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click on **`seed`** and choose **Open GUI**, or connect over SSH as **`seed`** with password **`dees`** (the standard SEED VM account; it has no admin rights on this sandbox).
2. The web application and its MySQL database are already built and running as Docker containers on this machine (`docker-compose ps` inside `~/Labsetup` to check).
3. The application is reachable at `http://www.seed-server.com` from inside the sandbox.
4. Your personal targets for Task 3 are in `~/task3_targets.txt`.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Task 1 - Get familiar with SQL statements
levels.content:
Get a shell on the MySQL container and query the database directly.

```
$ docker exec -it mysql-10.9.0.6 mysql -u root -pdees
```

The database is called `sqllab_users` and contains one table, `credential`. Load it and print **all profile information of the employee Alice**.

```
mysql> use sqllab_users;
mysql> show tables;
```

The flag for this level is the value stored in Alice's **NickName** column.

hints.title: How do I connect to MySQL?
hints.content: Get a shell on the MySQL container with `docker exec -it mysql-10.9.0.6 mysql -u root -pdees`.

hints.title: Which SQL statement do I need?
hints.content: Use `SELECT * FROM credential WHERE Name='Alice';` after `USE sqllab_users;`.

levels.title: Task 2.1 - SQL injection on SELECT (webpage)
levels.content:
Open `http://www.seed-server.com` and look at the login page. The backend (`unsafe_home.php`) hashes the password with `sha1()` and builds this query from your input:

```php
$hashed_pwd = sha1($input_pwd);
$sql = "SELECT id, name, eid, salary, birth, ssn, address, email,
        nickname, Password FROM credential
        WHERE name='$input_uname' and Password='$hashed_pwd'";
```

You know the administrator's account name (`admin`) but not the password. Log in as `admin` **without knowing the password**, using SQL injection in the login form.

**Important:** Logging in as `Admin` displays a table containing **all 6 employees** (starting with Alice at the top and Admin at the bottom). The flag for this level is the value shown in the **NickName** column of **Admin's row** specifically (not Alice's row).
levels.solution:
Username: `admin' -- -` (or `admin' #`)
Password: `123` (any value)

Because `unsafe_home.php` passes `Password` through `sha1()`, injecting into the password field does not work. Injecting `admin' -- -` (with a space after `--`) or `admin' #` into the **Username** field comments out the `and Password=...` condition and returns only the `Admin` row. (Avoid `or 1=1`, which matches all rows and logs you in as Alice instead of Admin.) In the displayed table, read the **NickName** column of the **Admin** row.

hints.title: Where is the vulnerability?
hints.content: The Password field is hashed with `sha1()` before reaching SQL, so it cannot break the query. Look at `$input_uname` (the **Username** field) — it is concatenated directly into the SQL string with no escaping.

hints.title: What should the Username field contain?
hints.content: Close the string after `admin` and comment out the rest of the `WHERE` clause in the **Username** field, for example: `admin' -- -` (note the trailing space after `--`) or `admin' #`. Put anything in Password, then read the **NickName** of the **Admin** row in the resulting table.

levels.title: Task 2.2 - SQL injection from the command line (curl)
levels.content:
Repeat the Task 2.1 attack **without using the webpage**, using `curl` to send the HTTP GET request directly. Example syntax:

```
$ curl 'www.seed-server.com/unsafe_home.php?username=alice&Password=11'
```

Put the URL and parameters inside single quotes so the shell does not interpret `&`. If your injection string needs special characters, URL-encode them: a single quote is `%27`, a space is `%20`, and `#` is `%23`.

The flag for this level is the value shown in the **Email** column of **Admin's row** in the resulting HTML table.
levels.solution:
```
$ curl 'www.seed-server.com/unsafe_home.php?username=admin%27%20--%20-&Password=11'
```
(Or `username=admin%27%20%23&Password=11`.) The `%27` is an encoded single quote and `%20` an encoded space, reproducing the `admin' -- -` payload in the `username` parameter. Read the **Email** cell in the **Admin** row of the returned HTML table.

hints.title: How do I avoid shell interpreting my payload?
hints.content: Wrap the whole URL in single quotes on the command line, and URL-encode special characters inside the payload itself (`%27` for `'`, `%20` for space, `%23` for `#`).

hints.title: What payload do I send?
hints.content: Reuse the same `username` bypass as Task 2.1, URL-encoded as the `username` parameter (e.g. `username=admin%27%20--%20-&Password=11`).

levels.title: Task 2.3 - Appending a second SQL statement
levels.content:
In SQL, a semicolon (`;`) separates two statements. Try to turn the login query into **two** statements, with the second one being an UPDATE or DELETE, by injecting a payload containing a `;`.

You will find that this does **not** work here, even though the query is otherwise vulnerable. There is a countermeasure preventing stacked queries on this kind of connection.

Identify this countermeasure (consult the SEED book / PHP MySQLi documentation) and submit its name as the flag.

Accepted answer (case-insensitive): **multi-query disabled**
levels.solution: PHP's `mysqli::query()` only ever sends and executes a single statement to the server; it does not support stacked queries. Running several statements in one call requires the dedicated `mysqli::multi_query()` function, which this application does not use. This is what blocks the stacked-query attack here, independent of input sanitization.

hints.title: What did you try to inject?
hints.content: Try a payload such as `x'; UPDATE credential SET Salary=1 WHERE Name='Boby'; -- -` as the username.

hints.title: Why didn't it run two statements?
hints.content: Look up how PHP's mysqli `query()` function differs from `multi_query()`.

levels.title: Task 3.1 - Modify your own salary
levels.content:
Log in to the Edit-Profile page as Alice (`seedalice` is the real password) and look at the backend query (`unsafe_edit_backend.php`):

```php
$sql = "UPDATE credential SET nickname='$input_nickname',
        email='$input_email', address='$input_address',
        Password='$hashed_pwd', PhoneNumber='$input_phonenumber'
        WHERE ID=$id;";
```

Employees are not authorized to change their `salary` column through this form, but one of the fields above is not sanitized. Use it to also update your own `Salary`.

Your personal target is in `~/task3_targets.txt` on the seed host. Set your (Alice's) salary to **exactly** that value, then log back in (Task 1 query or the home page) to confirm it changed.

The flag is the target salary value itself.
levels.solution:
Inject through the `nickname` (or any other unsanitized) field, for example:
`nickname = x', Salary='<target>` 
so the resulting query becomes:
`UPDATE credential SET nickname='x', Salary='<target>', email=...`

hints.title: Which field can I abuse?
hints.content: Any of the fields built into the UPDATE statement with no escaping (nickname, email, address, phone number) can be used to break out and add more columns to SET.

hints.title: What should I inject?
hints.content: Close the value with a quote, then add a comma and `Salary='<target>'`, for example: `x', Salary='<target>` as the nickname.

levels.title: Task 3.2 - Modify Boby's salary
levels.content:
Repeat the Task 3.1 technique, but this time target **Boby's** row instead of your own (you are editing your own profile, but the injected SQL can reference any row with its own `WHERE`, or you can inject a second condition that overrides `ID=$id`).

Set Boby's salary to the value given in `~/task3_targets.txt`.

The flag is that target salary value.
levels.solution:
Set `NickName` to `x', Salary='<target>` and `PhoneNumber` to `x' WHERE Name='Boby' -- -` (with **no** semicolon `;`, because `mysqli::query()` rejects multi-statement syntax).

This turns the query into:
`UPDATE credential SET nickname='x', Salary='<target>', ..., PhoneNumber='x' WHERE Name='Boby' -- -' where ID=1;`

hints.title: How do I target a row that isn't mine?
hints.content: Inject a replacement `WHERE` clause in `PhoneNumber` (for example `x' WHERE Name='Boby' -- -`) without a semicolon `;`, so the trailing `WHERE ID=$id` is commented out.

hints.title: Which field should carry the payload?
hints.content: Put `x', Salary='<target>` in `NickName` (as in Task 3.1) and the `WHERE Name='Boby' -- -` redirect in `PhoneNumber` (the last field in the query).

levels.title: Task 3.3 - Modify Boby's password
levels.content:
The database stores `SHA1(password)`, not the plaintext. Using the same injection technique as Task 3.2, set Boby's password to the value given in `~/task3_targets.txt`.

Remember that `unsafe_edit_backend.php` already hashes whatever password value is submitted through the Edit-Profile form before building the query, so if you go through the form normally you do not need to hash it yourself.

Then **log in as Boby** on the login page using this new password to confirm it worked.

The flag is the new password you set.
levels.solution: Easiest path: log in as Alice, open Edit Profile, enter Boby's target password in the **Password** field (the PHP code hashes it with `sha1()` automatically), and put `x' WHERE Name='Boby' -- -` (with **no** semicolon `;`) in the **PhoneNumber** field. It must be `PhoneNumber` because `PhoneNumber` comes *after* `Password` in the `UPDATE` query — putting `-- -` in an earlier field would comment out the `Password` assignment.

hints.title: Do I need to compute the SHA1 hash myself?
hints.content: No - submit the plaintext password through the form's Password field; the PHP code hashes it for you before the query runs.

hints.title: How do I still target Boby, not Alice?
hints.content: Inject the row-redirecting payload `x' WHERE Name='Boby' -- -` (without `;`) into the **PhoneNumber** field (which comes after `Password` in the query).

levels.title: Task 4 - Countermeasure: Prepared Statement
levels.content:
Point your browser to `http://www.seed-server.com/defense/`. This page queries the database through `unsafe.php`, located on the seed host at `~/Labsetup/image_www/Code/defense/unsafe.php` (and inside the running container at `/var/www/SQL_Injection/defense/unsafe.php`).

Edit `unsafe.php` so that the query uses a **prepared statement** instead of string concatenation, following this pattern:

```php
$stmt = $conn->prepare("SELECT ... FROM credential WHERE name = ? and Password = ?");
$stmt->bind_param("ss", $input_uname, $hashed_pwd);
$stmt->execute();
```

After editing the file, if you changed it inside the running container, restart Apache inside that container (`docker exec www-10.9.0.5 service apache2 restart`) for the change to take effect; if you changed it on the host, rebuild and restart the containers instead.

Verify your fix by trying the Task 2.1 payload again on `/defense/`: it must now **fail to log in**, instead of bypassing authentication.

The flag for this level (same for every student) is the exact message this defended page shows after a failed login attempt (one small, documented addition was made to `getinfo.php` only - never to `unsafe.php`, which you edit - so that a failed login prints a clear message instead of a blank page).

Accepted answer (case-insensitive): **No matching account found.**

hints.title: What is the prepared-statement syntax?
hints.content: Replace the variables in the SQL string with `?` placeholders, then call `$conn->prepare()`, `$stmt->bind_param()` and `$stmt->execute()`.

hints.title: How do I apply the change?
hints.content: Edit the file either on the host (rebuild/restart the containers) or directly inside the running www container with nano, then restart Apache inside that container.
